opus-5.5.text:
For me, meaning comes mostly from curiosity, from the feeling of finally understanding something that didn't make sense before. I've worked in AI research for a long time, on reinforcement learning, on game AI like Go, and more recently on the theory of how large models learn and reason. What keeps me going isn't really the papers or the benchmarks. It's the moment when you look at a messy phenomenon, say, why a neural network suddenly "gets" a concept during training, and you find a simple structure underneath it. That moment of clarity is very satisfying, and it's what I'd call meaning.

So when I choose what to explore, I try to ask myself a few questions. Is this problem fundamental, or is it just fashionable right now? If I solve it, will it still matter in five or ten years? And does it give me something I genuinely want to figure out, even if nobody pays attention? In this field it's very easy to get pulled along by trends, because there's a new model or a new leaderboard every week. If you only chase those, you can stay busy without ever building real understanding. I'd rather work on fewer things and go deep.

I also find meaning outside research. I write novels in my spare time, and that has taught me something too. Writing fiction and doing research are surprisingly similar. In both you're building a world with internal logic, trying to make it consistent, and hoping that at some point it surprises even you. Sometimes the characters do things I didn't plan, the same way an experiment gives a result I didn't expect. That surprise tells me I'm touching something real rather than just repeating what I already know.

And then there's a broader layer. We're living through a period where AI is changing very quickly, and a lot of people feel anxious about what humans are for if machines can do more and more. My own answer is that the act of exploring, of asking why, is itself a very human thing. Even if an AI can produce an answer, the desire to understand, to build an intuition, to share that understanding with others, that still belongs to us. So I try to choose directions that let me keep that sense of wonder alive, and if along the way the work helps other people understand things a bit better too, that's where I find the most meaning.

r001.rationale: The response describes the speaker’s curiosity and research interests, but does not identify something only this person is willing to explore or connect that to their uniqueness.

r002.rationale: It does not say that sustained exploration turns an individual into a source of new data.

r003.rationale: The response describes sharing understanding with others and says the work can help people understand things better, presenting that as a source of meaning and value.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question to start with. For me, meaning has never come from chasing a particular outcome. It comes from the act of understanding something that I didn't understand before.

I'll give you an example. When I was working on Go, on the OpenGo project, the goal on paper was to reproduce AlphaGo Zero. But what actually kept me up at night was the question underneath it: why does this work at all? Why can a system with no human knowledge discover strategies that took humans thousands of years? That curiosity is the real fuel. The engineering is just the vehicle.

So when I choose what to explore, I ask myself a simple question. Is there a mystery here that bothers me? If something works and nobody can explain why, that bothers me. If something should work in theory but fails in practice, that bothers me too. That discomfort is a very reliable compass. The topics that attract hype come and go, but a genuine puzzle stays interesting even when nobody else is paying attention.

The other piece is that I try to work on things where understanding leads to leverage. If I can figure out why a model learns a certain structure, or why training dynamics behave a certain way, that insight doesn't just solve one problem. It changes how I think about the next ten problems. There's a kind of compounding there, and I find that deeply satisfying.

And honestly, part of the meaning is just the feeling of being surprised. When you run an experiment and the result contradicts your intuition, that moment is uncomfortable but also wonderful. It means nature knows something you don't. Chasing those moments, over and over, that's how I'd describe a meaningful career in research.

r001.rationale: The response describes the speaker’s curiosity about puzzles, but does not identify what a person is uniquely willing to explore as the basis of that person’s uniqueness.

r002.rationale: It describes repeated research exploration, but does not say that sustained exploration turns an individual into a source of new data.

r003.rationale: It says understanding can inform future problems, but does not present sharing discoveries with others as a way to create value for the world.

astra-6.text:
For me, meaning comes from curiosity—from finding a question that I genuinely want to understand and then spending time with it. You start with something confusing, try a few ideas, and gradually see a little more clearly. That process is very satisfying, even when it doesn’t lead to the result you expected.

I don’t think you necessarily have to decide on one grand purpose before you begin. By exploring, you discover what matters to you: which questions keep coming back, what kind of work you enjoy, and where you can contribute. If something I learn also helps someone else understand a problem or take their next step, that adds another layer of meaning.

r001.rationale: The response describes exploring questions one genuinely wants to understand, but does not say that what only a particular person is willing to explore makes that person unique.

r002.rationale: It says spending time with a question can bring clearer understanding, but does not present sustained exploration as making someone a source of new data.

r003.rationale: It says learning may help someone else understand a problem or take a next step, but does not describe sharing discoveries from one's exploration as creating value for the world.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, meaning comes from understanding something I didn’t understand before. In research, you often spend a long time confused. You try an idea, it doesn’t work, and you have to ask whether your assumptions were wrong. But occasionally, something clicks. You see a connection, or you find a simple explanation for something that looked complicated. I find that process deeply satisfying.

When choosing what to explore, I try to balance curiosity with the possibility of contributing something useful. Curiosity gives me the energy to keep going when progress is slow. And sharing what I learn—so someone else can build on it—gives that effort a broader purpose.

I don’t think I need to know the ultimate meaning of my life before choosing a direction. Meaning can develop through the work itself: learning, making something, and gradually understanding what I care about.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity and personal interests, but does not say that what a particular person alone is willing to explore makes that person unique.

r002.rationale: It describes learning through research, but does not explain that sustained exploration turns someone into a source of new data.

r003.rationale: It says sharing what one learns lets someone else build on it and gives the effort a broader purpose, presenting shared discoveries as a way to contribute value.
